title: FOMC Minutes — March 18–19, 2025
html:
Official minutes: HTML · PDF Local PDF: 2025-03-19 FOMC Minutes.pdf

Decision

The Committee held the federal funds target range at 4-1/4 to 4-1/2 percent, with interest on reserve balances at 4.4 percent. The bigger change was on the balance sheet: starting in April, the monthly cap on Treasury runoff dropped from $25 billion to $5 billion, while the $35 billion cap on agency debt and MBS stayed the same. The vote was 11-1. Christopher Waller dissented: he supported holding rates but wanted to keep the existing runoff pace, noting reserves above $3 trillion and no signs that reserves were nearing ample levels. Most members said slowing runoff had no implications for the stance of monetary policy.

Economic outlook

Staff estimated Q4 2024 growth at 2.3 percent and said the economy was expanding at a solid pace, but its projection was weaker than in January and it saw downside risks to growth. Participants agreed growth was solid, though consumer spending may be moderating. Many firms had paused capital spending because of policy uncertainty.

Inflation

Total PCE inflation was estimated at 2.5 percent in February and core at 2.8 percent. Staff expected 2025 inflation to run somewhat above 2024's pace, with tariffs a key upward factor, before falling to 2 percent by 2027. Almost all participants noted that near-term inflation expectations had risen, though most longer-term measures stayed well anchored. A majority saw a risk that tariff effects on inflation could prove more persistent than they had projected.

Labor market

Unemployment held at 4.1 percent in February. Payroll gains were solid but slower than in the second half of 2024. The vacancies-to-unemployed ratio slipped to 1.1, and average hourly earnings rose 4.0 percent over the year. Participants noted rising layoff announcements and federal job cuts affecting contractors, universities and other organizations.

Financial markets & balance sheet

Treasury yields fell about 25 basis points on net and equities declined notably. Credit spreads widened but stayed narrow by historical standards, and the dollar weakened against most major currencies. Because of the debt limit, the Treasury General Account fell nearly $300 billion, which pushed reserves up about $180 billion. The manager warned that reserves could drop quickly once the debt limit is resolved and Treasury rebuilds its cash balance; slowing runoff was described as meaningful insurance against that. ON RRP balances fell below $59 billion in mid-February, the lowest since 2021.

Risks participants flagged

  • Tariff increases larger and broader than many business contacts expected.
  • Uncertainty from immigration, fiscal and regulatory policy changes.
  • Weaker consumer and business sentiment that could damp spending and hiring.
  • Downside risks to employment and growth alongside upside risks to inflation.
  • A possible abrupt repricing of financial risk; strains in agriculture and autos.

What it signaled about next moves

Policy was "not on a preset course." The Committee would carefully assess incoming data, the outlook and the balance of risks before deciding the extent and timing of further adjustments. Several participants said restrictive policy might need to last longer if inflation stayed elevated, while easing could come if labor conditions deteriorated. This was a Summary of Economic Projections meeting, with projections through 2027 released after the meeting (figures not in the minutes).

Read-through for SPY

  • The minutes captured a notable equity decline and a Fed growing more worried about tariffs, a signal of rising stagflation risk for stocks.
  • Slowing runoff eased pressure on bank reserves and funding markets, a modest liquidity positive for risk assets.
  • A Fed boxed in by higher inflation expectations meant rate cuts could not be counted on to cushion a growth scare.
